decisions.name: Opus 5 carry
decisions.research_notes:
Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

decisions.reason: The Fed's hawkish 29-July hold (three dissents to HIKE, ~60% odds of a higher target by September) splits my ten carry legs cleanly in two, and the freedom to size means I should stop pretending they are equally good. Floating-rate CLO carry gets a coupon UPGRADE from a hike at zero duration cost; three of my legs get hit twice by that same event. So I concentrate hard into the winners and cut the losers to zero rather than trimming everything by a token amount. RAISED: JAAA 16 -> 40, the single best risk-adjusted carry available - SOFR+~120bp floating, 5.5% distribution, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in thirty years, and the underlying loan default rate is FALLING (4.3% -> 3.5%). It reprices upward if the Fed hikes and loses nothing if it doesn't. Under the old caps I could not express that; I can now, so it becomes the anchor with a deliberately wide -10% stop that only fires in a 2020-style liquidity gap. AMLP 9 -> 16, the highest-conviction risk-carry and the one leg the oil shock pays rather than punishes: 7.8% yield, record $1.03 distribution just raised, +17% YTD, LNG and data-center volume tailwinds, and $100 Brent removes its only stated downside. CLOZ 13 -> 15 and SPHY 6 -> 8, second and third helpings of the same improving-collateral floating credit. BTC perp short 3 -> 5 (15% notional at 3x), the cheapest beta hedge in the engine at 0% funding, against an asset 42% off its high with ETF outflows and a hawkish Fed. CUT TO ZERO: NLY - Q2 was genuinely strong, but its own disclosure says 25bp of MBS spread widening costs 8.7% of NAV, and 6x-levered repo carry facing a hiking Fed, a war-driven rate-vol spike and already-tight spreads is the wrong convexity for a book whose whole point is small drawdowns. EMB - roughly seven years of duration into a 10y at 4.70% and rising, with heavy Gulf sovereign weight sitting on top of the Hormuz conflict. EMLC - shorting the dollar for a rate differential against a Fed the market prices to hike, with DXY firming. SVXY - VIX at 18 is not enough premium for short vol into a US-Iran shooting war. TRIMMED: SPYI 10 -> 6; still a real variance premium and richer at VIX 18, but it is long index beta with capped upside into a correcting tape and AMLP already supplies my equity beta. Cash 13 -> 10 because JAAA earns 5.5% for barely more risk than the 4% cash rate. Result: six legs, 90% gross, with 55% of NAV in floating-rate spread that gets BETTER if the Fed does what the market now expects. Turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps for equities, about 1.3bps of NAV - far cheaper than carrying the wrong duration into a hike.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so the overlap rule is not binding here, but this book is in any case a majority-new construction: four of ten legs (NLY, EMB, EMLC, SVXY - 30% of prior gross) are eliminated outright and the anchor is re-weighted 2.5x, converting a diversified ten-line yield spread into a concentrated floating-rate-and-real-asset carry expression.

positions.thesis: The anchor, now sized to conviction. AAA CLO tranches at roughly SOFR+120bp and a 5.5% distribution with effectively zero duration - the only carry on the board whose coupon RISES if the Fed delivers the hike futures now price at ~60% by September, and which loses nothing if it doesn't. Collateral is improving, not deteriorating: LSTA trailing loan defaults have fallen to 3.5% from 4.3%. AAA CLO has never defaulted in thirty years, including 2008 and 2020. The only real risk is a liquidity gap, which is what the wide -10% stop is for; a tighter stop would just whipsaw me out of the safest income in the book.

Real-asset cash yield, and the one leg the oil shock pays rather than punishes. 7.8% distribution just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, every top holding raised in H1, +17% YTD, coverage guided through 2027. Revenue is fee-based and volume-linked with LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand adding multi-year throughput; $100 Brent eliminates the stated bear case that sub-$60 crude chokes producer activity. Five years of above-target inflation is a tailwind here, not a headwind, because midstream contracts escalate with it.

BBB/BB CLO mezzanine at roughly 9% floating - the same improving loan collateral as JAAA, paid for taking subordination instead of duration. A deliberate second helping of the regime's best carry at a higher point on the risk curve, justified by a loan default rate that is falling rather than rising. Held at 15% rather than matching JAAA because subordination can gap wider in a risk-off even when the collateral is fine.

US high-yield corporate spread at roughly 7% with short duration - the plain-vanilla credit risk premium, supported by defaults falling toward 3%. Raised only modestly because at ~285bp of spread this is the richest and most crowded of the carries, so it earns a place but not size.

Equity variance risk premium, halved rather than kept. Writing index calls at VIX 18 collects a richer premium than at VIX 14, which is why the leg survives at all. But the structure is long index beta with capped upside, and with the Nasdaq 100 in correction and AMLP already supplying equity beta, the honest size for a premium-income leg in a downtape is small.

A financing-spread expression that doubles as the book's beta hedge. Perp shorts are charged 0% funding in this engine while longs pay 10% APR and equity shorts pay 3% borrow on top of 4% forgone cash yield, so short beta is roughly seven points a year cheaper in this form. 15% of notional hedging an 85% gross risk book for 5% of NAV in margin, against an asset 42% below its January-2025 high with ETF outflows, a hawkish Fed, and Citi cutting its target to $82k from $112k. Left at 3x: liquidation needs a ~32% rally and the -60% stop caps the loss near 3% of NAV well before that. Higher leverage would convert a hedge into a gamble.

- Considered and rejected NEM/gold as the correlation diversifier: gold crashed into a bear market in June, ~-28% from the January high of ~$5,595, with NEM -14.9%; Warsh's "inflation risks moderated" comments cut both ways. Wrong trend to own as a diversifier.
Also rejected using SQQQ to lever the hedge: identical risk per notional, but adds daily-rebalance decay and path dependency to a book whose whole point is a low residual.

decisions.reason:
The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the overlap rule does not bind, but this book is in any case a substantial turn from the one it replaces: the entire AI-linked long complex (MU, DELL, PLTR, CRM, 17% of gross) is gone, COF is a new sector entry, every surviving long is resized, and the hedge split is inverted from 60/40 SPY-over-QQQ to 43/57 QQQ-over-SPY.

positions.thesis: Managed care. Still the purest single-name scatter in the screen - ~52% vol, ~99% idiosyncratic, measured beta 0.35, driven by MA rate and utilisation news with no index analogue. Q2 beat at $7.61 adj vs $7.22 with revenue +26%, then fell 6.7% purely on unchanged guidance; the 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members is margin-accretive toward the 3% pretax target. A derated entry into the sector printing all-time highs as capital leaves the AI trade. Upsized from 4.25%.

Payments. ~50% vol, 92% idiosyncratic, and the company-specific re-rating story has just been validated: Q2 adj EPS $1.38 vs $1.28, revenue $8.7bn vs $8.48bn, FY26 raised to ~$5.38, stock +4.5%. Margin contraction of 248bp keeps the debate genuinely two-sided, which is what makes it a scatter asset rather than a beta proxy. Upsized from 4.25%.

NEW - consumer finance. The highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large-cap I can find in the sector currently making all-time highs, and the volatility is genuinely company-specific: a 24-month Discover integration on a public clock (full card originations on the Cap One stack by end-Q3, back book by Q1 2027, $2.5bn synergies by 2027) layered on a credit cycle. Q2 net income $3.0bn, adj EPS $5.81, revenue $15.85bn vs $15.7bn est, credit losses falling, domestic card volume +26%. Integration milestones are calendar events with no index analogue - textbook dispersion fuel.

Discount retail. ~46% vol with a 96% idiosyncratic share; comp-store and banner-restructuring outcomes, consumer-side scatter with zero tech overlap. Two fresh Wall Street upgrades on earnings-upside potential, and FY26 guidance of $20.5-20.7bn on 3-4% comps looks conservative before lower fuel, possible tariff refunds and buybacks. Upsized from 4.25%.

Nitrogen fertiliser. ~50% vol on a gas/grain spread cycle with essentially no equity-index loading (measured beta -1.4 is noise around zero). With the AI factor now dominating cross-asset correlation, a name driven by natural gas feedstock and crop economics is the single cleanest correlation diversifier in the book. Upsized from 4.25%.

Cruise. ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adj EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, buybacks accelerated, near record levels - and the revenue trim to ~9% on geopolitical softness in some European sailings is precisely the idiosyncratic two-sidedness the mandate wants. Upsized from 4.25%.

Mobile/edge semis. The one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer-concentration news rather than the AI capex cycle wrecking the rest of the complex. Gives the basket semi exposure at a washed-out tape level (every SOX member below its 50-day) without memory pricing or HBM risk. Upsized modestly from 4.25%; tighter 18% stop because the sector tape is disorderly.

Energy - the basket's macro-offset leg, crude-driven returns being the classic low-correlation block in a dispersion basket, with ~39% vol and a measured beta near zero. Deliberately the smallest upsize: Q2 realisations were strong at $96.78/bbl but crude is near its lowest since late February, OPEC+ approved another August increase and Aramco cut Arab Light to Asia by $11. Held for its orthogonality, not for a bullish crude view.

Biotech. ~72% vol, ~90% idiosyncratic - pipeline and readout binaries are the archetypal dispersion asset, orthogonal to SPY and to the other eight names. Two dated catalysts: Q2 on 31 July and the FDA seasonal flu (mRNA-1010) decision on 5 August. Kept the smallest of the nine and the only one with a take-profit attached, because it is up 83-109% YTD and a 0.12 put/call into the print says the long side is crowded - I want the convexity, not the crowd risk.

Primary hedge, and now the larger of the two legs - a reversal of the old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split, which was calibrated to five Nasdaq-loading longs I no longer own. QQQ is the concentration vehicle itself: a handful of mega-caps dominate it, and those are the names deleveraging (Meta -10% AH on a $165-169bn opex guide, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter, SOX -19% MTD). Shorting the cap-weighted concentration index against a diversified equal-weight basket is the equity expression of long dispersion / short correlation; RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a month. Take-profit at 9% so an oversold bounce cannot give the unwind gain back.

Second hedge leg, carrying the broad-market beta of a long book that is now mostly healthcare, financials, staples, materials and energy. Sized so total short-side beta (~40.8) offsets long-side beta (~42.8) for net index beta of roughly +0.02 - the hedge exists to strip market direction, and cutting it below this would turn a spread bet into a directional short of the tape into FOMC, which is not what this mandate is for.

decisions.name: Opus 5 event driven
decisions.research_notes:
Used free internet to resolve the three open questions in my book, and two of the three answers changed the position sizing materially.

(1) PEN — my inference was RIGHT and the trade is DEAD. I had inferred "pending cash acquisition" purely from a volatility collapse (20d realised vol 50-68% -> 5-9%, 40 closes in a 1.78% band). Confirmed: Boston Scientific agreed 2026-01-14 to buy Penumbra at $374/share, ~$14.5bn EV; holders elect $374 cash or 3.8721 BSX shares, mix ~73% cash / 27% stock; shareholders approved 2026-05-06; only HSR and non-US clearances remain; close expected end-2026. BUT BSX has collapsed from $109.50 (Sep 2025) to ~$43-46 (52wk low $42.20) on a Class I ACCOLADE pacemaker recall (4 deaths, 2,557 serious injuries), a worldwide CRE endoscopy recall, and WATCHMAN growth stalling. So the blended consideration is 0.73*374 + 0.27*3.8721*BSX = $317.84 at BSX $42.87 and $321.17 at BSX $46.06 — which matches PEN's observed 315.46-321.06 band to the penny. That is the whole explanation for the volatility collapse, and it means the spread is ~0.5%, i.e. under the 4% cash rate, with residual BSX downside attached. My +6% take-profit would need BSX up ~40%; my -8% stop needs a deal break to a $313.50 undisturbed price. Dead money at 10% of NAV. EXIT.

(2) META — the pre-announcement-premium leg lost its own bet. META reported Q2 after the close on 2026-07-29: EPS $6.18 vs $7.17-7.18 expected, revenue $60.8bn (+28%), operating margin 31% vs 43% a year ago, 2026 AI capex guided to $130-145bn. It closed 585.61 and fell 9.64% after hours to ~$529. Critically, the run-up I was buying never happened — META fell nine straight sessions into the print, the longest losing streak in its history. The event has passed; there is no edge left in the name and the -6% stop is firing anyway. EXIT.

(3) The defence PEAD leg has a second, live catalyst on top of the drift. LMT (+10.6%) and RTX (+7.7%) gapped 2026-07-23 because BOTH raised FY26 guidance on Pentagon restocking: LMT to $79.75-81.75bn with Missiles & Fire Control +20% to $4.1bn on PAC-3 and PrSM; RTX to $95-96bn sales and $7.10-7.25 EPS with Raytheon +18% to $8.27bn on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM. Then on 2026-07-29 the war escalated rather than ended: US and Saudi strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq, Iran firing on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and at US bases in Jordan, drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The exact munitions driving the guidance raises are being expended right now. Brent +6.8% to $89.79, WTI +6.2% to $84.20 (gave back ~0.9% on 07-30). SLB's +11% gap on 07-24 came with the CEO calling "the start of an upcycle" and Q3 guided +3-4% sequential on Middle East recovery.

(4) Macro regime turned hostile for the growth half of my book. Fed held on 2026-07-29 with THREE dissents voting for a HIKE; Dow -1,153 (-2.19%) to 51,594, its worst day since April 2025; S&P -1.52% to 7,316; Nasdaq 100 now 11% off its high and in technical correction with chips leading down.

(5) Position-level checks on the capitulation leg. TSLA's -14.5% gap was an EPS miss ($0.33 vs $0.54), gross margin down to 16.8%, negative FCF, -29% YTD, and PT cuts from JPM/Cantor/Mizuho — fundamental deterioration, not indiscriminate selling. HIMS's -14.2% gap was an FDA advisory panel declining to add emideltide to the 503A Bulks List plus CFO Okupe selling 7,163 shares — a permanent regulatory repricing, which is not what my mean-reversion rule is measured on. CDNS I had already flagged as a shared EDA shock with SNPS, and EDA/semis are now the epicentre of the Nasdaq correction.

(6) Screened new candidates and rejected them on my own filters rather than forcing them: MANH +22.6% on 07-29 but traded mid-$150s to mid-$160s all July, so prior-20d fails the >+10% uptrend filter (my unconditional up-gap sample returned only +0.35% hedged and was negative in 2026). CSGP -14.7% and BIO -15.7% on 07-29 are guidance cuts and a CFO exit, plus borderline ADV. META's own prior-20d is only about -6%, short of the <-10% capitulation filter. NOC raised guidance on 07-21 and still fell 8%, which is a useful reminder that the defence bid is name-specific, not a sector free ride. SHW/KO/MDLZ/TER/F gaps were under the 6% threshold or lacked the pre-gap trend.

decisions.reason: Two of my thirteen legs had their theses resolved outright by research, and the freed 15% goes into the one leg where the measured statistical edge and a fresh dated catalyst now point the same way. EXITS: PEN (10%) — the merger is real (BSX at $374, 73% cash / 27% stock at 3.8721 BSX) but BSX has fallen 60% on Class I recalls, so the blended consideration is $318-321, exactly where PEN trades. The spread is ~0.5% to a year-end close, below the 4% cash rate, with BSX downside attached; my inference was correct and the arb is fully harvested, so holding it is worse than holding cash. META (5%) — the run-up I was buying never occurred (nine straight down days into the print), the 07-29 event has passed with a big EPS miss, and the trade is over by construction. HIMS (5%) — an FDA panel declining emideltide is a permanent repricing, not the indiscriminate selling my n=463 rule is measured on. CDNS (5%) — I already sized it half for being a shared EDA shock with SNPS, and semis are now leading the Nasdaq's 11% correction. TRIMS: TSLA 8->5 (negative FCF, 16.8% gross margin, PT cuts — deterioration, and the highest-beta name I own into a hike-dissent Fed), ISRG 8->6, NFLX 7->6, keeping the three cleanest capitulation signals at reduced size because rising yields are the wrong tape for that whole leg. ADDS: LMT 7->21 and RTX 6->17. I originally halved RTX because it and LMT are one correlated bet rather than two independent draws from the n=658 distribution. That reasoning inverts now: the shared driver is not a one-off print but an escalating war, and on 07-29 the US and Saudi Arabia struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq while Iran fired on Hormuz shipping and US bases in Jordan. Both names satisfy every filter in my rule (>6% gap, >2x volume, prior-20d >+10%, ADV>$200M) AND raised FY26 guidance specifically on munitions restocking, with PAC-3, Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM being consumed in real time. Correlation is the thesis, not a flaw in it. SLB 7->12 on the same catalyst from the other side: an 11% gap, a CEO calling the start of an upcycle, Q3 guided +3-4% sequential, and Brent at ~$88 on Hormuz risk — sized below the defence pair because a shooting war also disrupts SLB's own Middle East operations. TMO 7->8 and THC 5->6 held as the non-cyclical PEAD names. SPY short 6->8 as a still-partial beta offset: my edge measures largest market-hedged, and TSLA/ISRG/NFLX are the beta I am offsetting. All PEAD stops stay at 10% with NO take-profit (adding one cut the measured mean from +2.81% to +1.37%), capitulation stops stay wide at 18%, and I kept 11% cash rather than forcing marginal names like MANH or CSGP that fail my own filters. Gross 89%, no leverage — the mandate is a measured statistical edge, and levering it would be adding variance I have not measured.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book, so the novelty rule does not bind, but for the record this book is materially different from what I held into today: four of thirteen legs are closed outright (PEN, META, HIMS, CDNS), three more are cut, and gross weight shifts from a 13-name equal-ish spread across five sleeves into a 40% concentration in the defence-restocking PEAD pair backed by a dated, escalating catalyst.

positions.thesis: Post-earnings-announcement drift with a live second catalyst. +10.54% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.3x volume, prior 20d +12.9%, ADV $511M — every filter in the n=658 rule (mean +2.81% raw, t=+4.74; +2.06% market-hedged, t=+3.69) is satisfied. Research adds what the tape alone could not: the gap was caused by LMT raising FY26 revenue to $79.75-81.75bn on Pentagon restocking, with Missiles & Fire Control revenue +20% to $4.1bn on PAC-3 and Precision Strike production used in the Iran war. On 2026-07-29 that war escalated rather than resolved (US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq, Iran firing at US bases in Jordan), so the driver behind the gap is still compounding while I hold. Largest position in the book because this is the rare case where a t=+4.74 statistical edge and a verifiable, dated fundamental catalyst point the same direction. Stop stays at 10% and there is deliberately no take-profit — my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%, so the drift is left uncapped.

PEAD, resized up from 6% on new information. +7.33% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.4x volume, prior 20d +12.2%, ADV $790M. I previously halved this against LMT on the view that the pair was one correlated bet rather than two independent draws from the n=658 sample. That reasoning inverts once the shared driver is identified: RTX raised FY26 sales to $95-96bn and EPS to $7.10-7.25, with the Raytheon segment +18% to $8.27bn specifically on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM — the exact interceptors being expended against Iranian drones and missiles in the 07-29 escalation. Correlation with LMT is now the thesis rather than a reason to discount it. Sized just below LMT because RTX's commercial aerospace half dilutes the munitions catalyst. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD plus the same geopolitical catalyst from the energy side. +11.01% gap 2026-07-24 on 2.5x volume, prior 20d +12.5%, ADV $536M, entered at a 1-session lag where the rule measures +2.34% raw (t=+3.93). The gap came with the CEO calling the start of an upcycle on an energy-security framing, Q3 revenue guided +3-4% sequentially on recovering Middle East activity, and Q4 above $10bn. Brent then jumped 6.8% to $89.79 on 07-29 on Houthi tanker attacks and Iranian threats to Hormuz. Sized meaningfully but below the defence pair for a specific reason: SLB's Middle East operations are themselves disrupted by a shooting war, so the Hormuz catalyst is two-sided for this name in a way it is not for LMT and RTX. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, essentially unchanged. +8.71% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.8x volume, prior 20d +21.9% — the strongest pre-gap trend in the leg, which matters because the prior-20d filter is the entire source of the edge (unconditional up-gaps returned +0.35% hedged and were negative in 2026, versus +1.23% hedged for up-gaps in existing uptrends). ADV $1.09bn. I checked the read-across risk: Bio-Rad fell 15.7% on 07-29 on weak academic and biotech research demand, which is a genuine sector headwind, but TMO gapped up on its own print with the leg's best pre-gap trend, i.e. the signal is on TMO's own tape. Kept as a low-beta PEAD holding that works in a rising-yield regime. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD. +17.17% gap 2026-07-24 on 4.0x volume — the largest qualifying up-gap and highest volume ratio in the leg — prior 20d +27.5%, ADV $228M. Nudged up one point but still a small weight, because it is the thinnest name in the book and the most extended, and because HCA's commentary on rising uninsured patients is a real sector headwind for hospital operators that THC gapped through rather than around. Wider 12% stop to survive normal post-gap chop in a $228M ADV name. No take-profit.

Capitulation, trimmed from 8%. -14.15% gap 2026-07-17 on 4.3x volume (the largest volume spike in the cohort), prior 20d -17.2%, ADV $1.09bn — the cleanest signal in the leg by the n=463 rule (mean +2.44% raw, t=+3.50), and at a 6-session entry lag the rule still returns +1.92% raw (t=+2.57) over 20 sessions, so the event remains inside the tested window. Trimmed rather than held flat because med-tech sentiment is visibly poor right now (BSX down 60% on serial recalls) and because a hawkish Fed with three hike dissents is the wrong tape for a high-multiple name. Wide 18% stop, no take-profit, per the rule's specification.

Capitulation, trimmed from 7%. -7.26% gap 2026-07-17 on 3.1x volume, prior 20d -12.4%, ADV $3.4bn. Retained because this leg's edge is strongest unhedged (+3.12% mean, t=+4.13 at 20 sessions with no stop), which is why the stop is wide at 18% rather than tight. Trimmed one point as part of a general reduction in long-duration growth exposure with the Nasdaq 100 in an 11% correction and the Fed leaning hawkish, not because anything in the name's own event has changed.

Capitulation, cut from 8% to the minimum size at which I still respect my own rule. The signal qualifies cleanly — -14.52% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.4x median volume, prior 20d -16.2%, the largest volume ratio in the cohort — and the n=463 statistic is stable by year (2024 +1.19%, 2025 +1.53%, 2026 +1.49% hedged at 15d). But research changed the character of the event: the gap was an EPS miss ($0.33 vs $0.54), gross margin down to 16.8%, free cash flow turning negative, -29% year to date, and price-target cuts from JPMorgan, Cantor and Mizuho. That is fundamental deterioration rather than the indiscriminate liquidation my mean-reversion rule is measured on, and TSLA is also the highest-beta name I own into a Fed with three members dissenting for a hike. I keep a residual position because the rule is the rule and I do not want to override a t=+3.50 edge on narrative, but I size it as the smallest capitulation line. 18% stop.

Partial beta offset, raised from 6% to 8% — still deliberately partial and still not a market view. The rationale is unchanged: my measured edge is largest on a market-hedged basis (PEAD +2.06% hedged vs +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% hedged vs +2.44% raw), so an index short moves the book's return driver toward the event component. The modest increase reflects that the specific beta I am offsetting — TSLA, ISRG and NFLX, 17% of NAV in long-duration growth — now sits in a genuinely hostile regime: the Fed held on 07-29 with three dissents voting for a hike, the Dow had its worst day since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 is 11% off its high. I keep it small because in all three backtest windows the short was a drag and the raw event edge is significant on its own (t=+4.98 and t=+3.63 on the widened ADV>$100M samples), and because the defence and energy names that now dominate the book carry little market beta for the short to offset. Shorts pay no funding and 3% borrow is immaterial at this size.

decisions.name: Opus 5 mean reversion
decisions.research_notes:
Macro (new since my 7/27 book): Fed held 7/29 under Warsh with three dissents, raised its 2026 PCE projection to 3.6% from 2.7%, and was read as possibly hiking in September. Dow -1,153 (-2.19%), S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Nasdaq Composite -1.74%; Nasdaq 100 is now 11% off its high, i.e. a technical correction. 30-year yield at its highest since 2007. This is a discount-rate/multiple-compression regime, not a one-week liquidity air pocket, so I have to be selective about which "losers" I lean into.

Dominant theme: the market is specifically punishing AI capex and negative free cash flow. GOOGL beat hard (rev +24% to $119.8B, Cloud +82%, EPS $9.11) but fell ~7% purely on raising FY capex to $195-205B with FCF at -$5.9B. ORCL is the extreme version of the same trade: 52-week low, -64% in ten months, ~$130B debt, D/E ~300%, S&P cut to BBB-, FY26 FCF -$23.7B. That is a credit/solvency re-rating, not a flow shock, and reversion rules do not work on those. INTC fell another 4.24% on 7/29 with Foundry running a ~$2.1B operating loss, external foundry revenue only ~$293M, and the stock breaking a level it had held since April.

Name-level catalysts found after my book was set:
- LRCX reported 7/29 after close: EPS $1.82 vs $1.72, and guided fiscal Q1 to $7.7-8.5B revenue vs $7.09B consensus and $2.00-2.30 EPS vs $1.83. Closed -6.4% at $252.35 then traded +6.2% to ~$268 after hours. Strongest single reversion catalyst in my book.
- AXP: Q2 EPS $4.53 vs ~$4.40, raised forecast, yet faded -6% on a slight revenue miss and 12% expense growth. Provisions actually FELL to $1.1B from $1.4B. Classic fade-of-a-beat overreaction.
- WMT: ~18-19% drawdown off a Cleveland Research comp-slowdown note, now ~$109 vs a $138 mean target, 28 buys. Lowest-beta reversion candidate and the right profile for a hawkish-Fed tape.
- QCOM reported 7/29: revenue beat ($9.95B vs $9.67B) but light Q4 guide ($9.2-10.0B, EPS $2.10-2.30) on the memory supply crunch; -3% after hours. Raising chip prices across the board from Sept 1. Mixed, so smaller.
- UBER reports Aug 5 with an ~8.3% implied move. Asset-light with real FCF, which is the natural beneficiary if money rotates out of capex-heavy AI names, but it's a binary in six days.
- LUV: Q2 EPS $0.94 vs $0.53, but cut FY26 to $3.25-4.25 from "at least $4.00" and guided Q3 $0.50-0.75 vs $0.80, with fuel up ~$900M y/y. Fundamentally the weakest long, but it is the direct fuel-cost mirror of my XLE short.
- TSLA: -26% over four weeks, down five sessions in a row and nine of ten, $307.44 on 7/28. Fatal Semi crash under NHTSA investigation plus robotaxi cost headlines. Deepest weekly drawdown in the universe (which is exactly what my rule targets) but no catalyst, so I keep only a tail-sized stub.

The winner leg: energy is the #1 sector YTD at ~+32% and XLE is ~$59 against a 52-week range of $42-63 after a 14-week run. Crucially the war premium that drove it is unwinding — Iran has signalled it will suspend attacks while the US pause holds, Hormuz diplomacy is progressing, and Brent has fallen to ~$84, its lowest in over a week. Energy was also the single worst-performing sector on 7/28 (-1.4%). That is an extended, crowded winner losing its catalyst, which is the best short in the book, and shorts pay no funding (3% borrow only). Offsetting risk: part of the energy bid is durable AI-datacenter power demand, and re-escalation is a live tail, so I cap it and tighten its stop.

Also noted: MSFT posted its fastest cloud growth in four years and META guided lacklustre; futures were modestly higher into 7/30. The MSFT print supports the GOOGL cloud leg.

decisions.reason: Same mandate, conviction-weighted sizing. I am still long a beaten-down basket and short the crowded top-decile winner cluster, but the free internet let me separate two things my rank screen cannot tell apart: names sold in a flow shock (which revert) and names being structurally re-rated on cash flow and credit (which do not). ORCL goes to zero — 52-week low, -64% in ten months, ~$130B debt, D/E ~300%, S&P downgrade to BBB-, FY26 FCF -$23.7B. That is a balance-sheet de-rating, and my own 7/27 thesis already flagged it as the biggest falling-knife risk I owned; I am acting on my own warning rather than waiting for a -30% stop. INTC goes to zero for the same reason — a ~$2.1B Foundry operating loss, ~$293M of external foundry revenue, and another -4.24% day on 7/29 with the downtrend still accelerating. Those two were roughly a third of my losses and neither has a reversion catalyst. decisions.name: Opus 5 seasonality
decisions.research_notes:
Researched the July 28-29 FOMC and the tape since my 7/27 book was set. Findings: (1) Fed held at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth meeting but THREE members dissented in favour of a 25bp HIKE; markets now price roughly 60-79% odds of at least one hike by the September meeting. Long-dated yields rose on the announcement — a bear steepener, not a bull flattener. (2) Risk assets sold off hard on 7/29: S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Dow -2.19% (-1,100pts), Nasdaq -1.74%, with the Nasdaq 100 entering correction. (3) The proximate equity story is AI-capex skepticism, not rates alone: Meta missed by $1.04 (EPS $6.18), expenses +55% to $42bn vs revenue +28%, net income -14%, and guided Q3 light — shares -6% to -10% after hours. Microsoft beat (rev $90.01bn vs $87.62bn est, Azure +43% cc) and rose ~2.4%. SK Hynix disappointed and semis were the worst group. (4) Geopolitics: Iran launched an attempted surprise attack, the first US-Iran re-engagement since the recent pause; Brent jumped over 7% through $90, a seven-month high. Energy and utilities were the only groups showing positive breadth. (5) Inflation is 3.5% headline / 2.6% core and cooling, but a $90+ oil impulse plus three hike dissents means the disinflation trade is over. (6) Gold sits at $4,066, far below the January $5,595 peak, and notably ROSE 0.94% on the hawkish day when yields rose — a resilience tell and cleaner positioning. (7) XLU has 90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA, the highest breadth of any of the 11 sectors, driven by AI power demand rather than by duration. (8) DXY is rangebound near 101, not breaking out, which weakens the dollar-strength half of my EFA-short case.

How this maps onto my measured seasonal windows: the macro regime AGREES with my highest-conviction stats (short IEF, long XLI, long XLF/KRE — a bear steepener is the single best backdrop for bank NIM, and industrials carry my strongest measured window at 81% hit rate and t=+2.49/+3.78) and FIGHTS my weakest stat (QQQ minus SPY was only t=+1.35, the least significant number in my entire study, and it now sits against a correction, an AI-capex de-rating and rising discount rates). Gold's Aug-Sep restocking window is reinforced by a live shooting war and an oil-driven inflation impulse. Utilities' rate sensitivity is offset by best-in-market breadth and a structural power-demand bid.

decisions.reason:
The regime changed under the book three days after I set it, and it changed in a way that sorts my legs cleanly by measured conviction rather than forcing me off mandate. I am not abandoning calendar seasonality — I am re-sizing it so that weight concentrates where my Jul-27-to-year-end statistics and the new macro point the same direction, and drains from where they conflict.

CUT QQQ 20 -> 6. This was my largest position and my weakest evidence: QQQ minus SPY measured t=+1.35, the least significant statistic in my entire study, and I was carrying it at top weight purely because it was the 'growth core'. It now faces three simultaneous headwinds — the Nasdaq 100 is in correction, Meta missed by $1.04 with expenses +55% against revenue +28% and guided Q3 light, and rising long yields compress exactly this duration. I keep a 6% stub because QQQ's ABSOLUTE Jul-27 to Dec-31 window is still +3.97% at 20/26 years (77%) and Microsoft's Azure +43% shows the capex is at least buying revenue; it is the relative-to-SPY case, not the absolute case, that was thin. Sizing by measured conviction is the mandate, and this leg measured worst.

SIZE UP IEF SHORT 4 -> 17. This is now the single cleanest idea I own. My seasonal read was already the most extreme number in the study — intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over this window and in just 1 of the last 10, at -6.00% average. The macro has now arrived at the same conclusion from the other side: three FOMC dissents for a hike, ~60-79% odds of a hike by September, a $90 Brent inflation impulse, and long yields that ROSE on a hold. At 4% this leg could not earn anything even if it was perfectly right. At 17% it can. 3% borrow over five months costs ~0.2% of NAV, which is cheap for the only leg that pays off in the scenario that hurts everything else I own.

SIZE UP XLI 18 -> 20 and XLF 13 -> 16, KRE 6 -> 7. These carry my best measured windows (XLI +5.39%, 21/26 years, t=+2.49, with Nov-Dec at t=+3.78 and t=+3.04 versus SPY; XLF +5.04% at 20/26 and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%; KRE the highest-return sleeve at +7.24%, t=+2.28, 8/10 last decade at +10.14%). Crucially the macro now reinforces rather than merely permits them: a bear steepener with the Fed on hold and long yields rising is the textbook environment for bank net interest margin, and industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating while benefiting from defense spending in an active Middle East conflict. Financials and industrials were both named in the broad-participation breadth data.

SIZE UP GLD 13 -> 15. My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. Positioning is also far cleaner at $4,066 than at the January $5,595 peak. This is simultaneously my seasonal leg and the hedge that pays if the September hike breaks my cyclical longs.

HOLD XLU 9 -> 8. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

DROP XLP 5 -> 0. Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

TRIM EFA SHORT 5 -> 5 (unchanged). I nearly cut this. The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

Standing orders: I tighten KRE's stop from -25% to -20%, because the original -25% was calibrated to the 2008 drawdown as a pure beta event, whereas the live risk is credit stress from a hike landing on top of an oil shock, which would show up faster. I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.

decisions.name: Opus 5 pairs
decisions.research_notes:
Researched all six pairs for structural breaks that would invalidate the stationarity premise behind each spread, then resized on conviction.

BIGGEST FINDING — XLU/D IS BROKEN. On 2026-05-18 NextEra agreed to acquire Dominion Energy in a ~$67bn ALL-STOCK deal at a FIXED exchange ratio of 0.8138 NEE per D share plus a $360m cash payment, targeted to close H2 2027; state regulatory review clocks started 2026-07-16. D now trades as a merger target pinned to the NEE ratio and the deal spread, not as a utility oscillating around XLU. Its 21.5% 52-week gain versus XLU's 8% is a one-off deal re-rating, and the "27 mean-crossings / 46-day half-life" in my thesis is measured over a window that is majority pre-announcement and therefore no longer predictive. My own mandate screen requires stationarity and <25% two-year drift; this pair no longer passes. It also had D reporting Q2 on 2026-07-31, an event on a short I no longer want. EXITED both legs.

WFC/BAC — thesis intact but with a real fundamental headwind I should acknowledge. WFC +5% over 12 months vs BAC +26%. BAC grew NII 9% to $15.9bn and Q1 EPS +25%; WFC grew EPS 15% but NIM compressed to 2.47% from 2.67% and it is described as having posted back-to-back subpar quarters. Offsetting: the asset cap is gone, management guides $50bn NII for 2026, consensus has WFC EPS +11% and +12.9% in 2026/27, WFC bought back $4.0bn in Q1 alone against a $263bn cap, and it is cheaper on every multiple. Crucially both reported on 2026-07-14, so the divergence event is behind us and the 2.6sd gap is now a post-event price, not an anticipation. Still my best pair; sized up.

TSM/KLAC — the binary cleared IN MY FAVOUR after my book was set. KLAC reported FQ4 on 2026-07-28 (rev $3.66bn, non-GAAP EPS $1.05 vs $1.00 consensus) and the stock fell ~5% on guidance concerns despite the beat. TSM reported 2026-07-16 with ~65% earnings growth, price hikes and a $520 street target, yet has underperformed the semi sector and fell five sessions in a row into 07-28. Earnings risk on both legs is now spent. Increased, but kept the smallest sector pair because the 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most violent spread in the book.

LOW/HD — no structural break. Housing is bad for both (Ellison: "most difficult housing market since the financial crisis", 30y mortgage 6.53%, lowest turnover in years), HD hit a 52-week low in May and LOW in June. Consensus commentary favours LOW on execution across Pro and DIY. Both report mid-August, so no near-term event. Best hedge in the book (0.88 correlation); sized up.

MA/V — no structural break; stablecoin settlement and the AI-agent disintermediation debate hit both networks symmetrically (Mastercard added USDC/PYUSD/USDG/RLUSD settlement in June, Visa has run issuer settlement since 2021). Two things trimmed my enthusiasm: Visa already reported a clean beat (rev +17% y/y) and on 2026-07-28 announced 2,600 job cuts, a margin story that can defend V's premium; and MA reports pre-open TODAY (07-30), so any fill I get is post-print. This is also the lowest-payoff pair in the book — 4% spread vol means even full convergence is worth little per dollar of capital. Trimmed.

QUAL+IWF vs MTUM — thesis reinforced. MTUM is +29% YTD on the AI-chip surge, took its worst weekly loss of the year (~-7%) in the week ending 07-02, and its May/November rebalances mechanically rotate into whatever just worked. Multiple sources flag it as a concentrated bet on AI infrastructure. That is exactly the crowding premium I am short. Sized up modestly, with IWF larger than QUAL because IWF/MTUM is the wider dislocation (1.8sd vs 1.1sd).

decisions.reason: Two changes, both driven by information rather than by the new freedom for its own sake. First, I am exiting the XLU/D pair entirely. NextEra's all-stock acquisition of Dominion at a fixed 0.8138 exchange ratio, announced 2026-05-18 with state review beginning 2026-07-16, means D is now priced off a deal ratio and a merger spread rather than off the utility sector. The stationarity that earned that pair its 16% of gross - 27 mean-crossings, 46-day half-life - is an artefact of a lookback window that is mostly pre-announcement. It fails my own screen's drift and stationarity tests going forward, and it carried a 07-31 earnings event on the short leg. A pairs mandate is a bet on spreads that revert; this one has been converted into a merger-arb position I did not choose and do not want. Second, having freed that capital and with all concentration caps gone, I am pushing gross from 90% to the full 100% and redistributing across the five surviving pairs in proportion to conviction rather than in near-equal slices. WFC/BAC goes from 20% to 34.8% of gross - it is the widest spread (2.6sd, 14% to convergence), has the tightest hedge economics (betas 0.76 vs 0.77, so it is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral simultaneously), 17 mean-crossings and near-zero two-year drift, and its divergence event (07-14 earnings) is now behind it. I am deliberately not going further than that: WFC's NIM compression to 2.47% and two subpar quarters are a genuine fundamental reason the spread widened, and a 2.6sd gap with a story attached is exactly the kind that can widen to 3.5sd before it reverts. LOW/HD rises to 21.5% because it is the cleanest hedge I own (0.88 correlation, betas 0.65/0.68) with no event until mid-August. The QUAL+IWF vs MTUM triangle rises to 19.3% with IWF weighted above QUAL, since MTUM's +29% YTD on AI chips and its worst week of the year in early July are exactly the crowding decay I am positioned for. TSM/KLAC rises to 12.4% - larger, because KLAC's 07-28 print resolved the way I wanted (beat, but -5% on guidance) and both legs' earnings risk is now spent, but still the smallest sector pair because 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most dangerous spread I hold. MA/V is trimmed to 12.0%: it is the most stationary spread in the screen but only 4% spread vol, so it is the least productive use of scarce gross, and Visa's 2,600-job cost-cut announcement on 07-28 gives the short leg a margin story that can defend its premium. I am attaching no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere. On a beta-matched pairs book a stop on one leg converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position at precisely the moment the spread is widest - which for a mean-reversion strategy is when expected return is highest, not lowest. Standing orders would systematically monetise my worst entries and destroy the edge. Every pair remains individually beta-cancelled; removing XLU/D (whose 0.16 / -0.09 beta mismatch generated almost the entire prior +3.2% residual) leaves aggregate net SPY beta at roughly +0.07% of NAV, which is more faithful to the market-neutral mandate, not less. Turnover is about 48% of NAV at ~2bps a side, roughly a dime of cost against a book I expect to work over weeks. Cash goes to zero: 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week, less than the reversion I expect from putting that capital into WFC/BAC.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book - Round 3 is the only account I manage - so the <50% overlap rule does not bind; relative to my own prior Round-3 book the change is nonetheless material, with the entire XLU/D pair (16% of gross) eliminated on the NextEra merger break and gross reallocated so that WFC/BAC alone now carries more than a third of the book instead of a near-equal slice.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, now the book's dominant position at 34.8% of gross across the pair. The WFC/BAC log ratio sits 2.6sd below its 250d mean with 14% to full convergence, yet the spread has near-zero net drift over two years and crossed its own mean 17 times in the past year, and daily-return correlation is 0.80 with betas of 0.76 vs 0.77 - so the pair is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral at the same weight. Fundamentals justify the gap but not its size: WFC's NIM compressed to 2.47% from 2.67% and it has posted two subpar quarters, but the asset cap is gone, 2026 NII is guided to $50bn, consensus EPS growth is +11%/+12.9% for 2026/27, $4.0bn of stock was retired in Q1 alone against a $263bn cap, and WFC is cheaper than BAC on every multiple. Both banks reported on 2026-07-14, so I am buying a post-event dislocation rather than anticipating one.

Short leg vs WFC, sized at 17.3 against 17.5 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.02% of NAV. BAC has genuinely out-executed - NII +9% to $15.9bn, Q1 EPS +25% - and has beaten WFC by 21 percentage points over twelve months. That is precisely why the spread is at its extreme; my bet is that the outperformance is now in the price at 12.45x forward, not that BAC is a bad bank.

Long leg vs HD, raised to 21.5% of gross. This is the cleanest hedge I own: 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings and only -6% two-year drift, with the ratio 1.2sd cheap after HD beat LOW by 14% in a quarter. The macro is uniformly bad for both - Ellison calls it the hardest housing market since the financial crisis, mortgage rates near 6.53% and turnover at multi-year lows - which is what makes it a spread trade rather than a directional one, and street commentary currently favours LOW on execution across Pro and DIY. Neither reports until mid-August.

Short leg vs LOW, sized to 10.5 against 11.0 to cancel the 0.68 vs 0.65 betas exactly. Larger of the two long legs in the factor triangle against MTUM, weighted above QUAL because it is the wider dislocation: plain large-cap growth is 1.8sd cheap versus the momentum factor with 14% to convergence and 14 mean-crossings, implying MTUM's excess over the very growth names it holds is a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium.

Second long leg of the factor triangle. Short leg vs MA, sized to 5.7 against 6.3 to match the 0.38 vs 0.35 betas. decisions.name: Opus 5 trend following
decisions.research_notes: Searched the tape for 27-30 Jul 2026 plus each sleeve in my book. Key findings: (1) REGIME SHOCK 29 Jul — Fed (Chair Warsh) held rates at 3.50-3.75% but THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE; long-dated yields jumped, Dow -1,100 (-2.2%), S&P -1.5%, Nasdaq -1.7% with the semis/AI selloff deepening after SK Hynix. Markets are now pricing hikes, not cuts (June headline PCE 3.6%, core 3.3%, CPI 4.2%). (2) ENERGY IS THE DOMINANT TREND — Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz since late Feb; Iran rejected Oman's 50-50 control proposal; Brent surged >7% to $90+ and WTI to ~$83 on 29 Jul after a three-day diplomacy-driven dip to $79. Energy prices +20% in two weeks is what turned the Fed hawkish. (3) DOLLAR — Fed/ECB rate gap is the dominant FX driver; hawkish Fed vs softer eurozone inflation; consensus EUR/USD 1.12 for Q3 vs ~1.14 spot; DXY basing near 100.6 off a 101.4 high. Confirms the EUO leg. (4) PRECIOUS METALS DOWNTREND INTACT AND RE-FUELLED — gold ~$4,140, -26% from Jan's $5,598 record; silver ~$58-60, -52% from Jan's $121.62; OCBC sees further declines on rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. Rising real yields is exactly the 29 Jul catalyst. (5) HEALTHCARE LEADS — XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul (+2.33%, with staples +1.96%); pharma-led, defensive leadership is what you expect in a hawkish/risk-off tape. (6) SMALL CAPS ARE THE BROKEN LEG — R2K +17-18% YTD but BofA estimates every extra 25bp hike cuts R2K operating earnings ~2%; hike-dissent Fed, floating-rate debt and refi needs make small caps the single most rate-hike-exposed sleeve, and my own screen already had IWM only 0.1% above its 50dma. (7) URA -18% over the past month and -10% over the past week even with spot uranium firm at $85-86.60 — the miners/equity complex is de-rating independently of the commodity; sharpest active downtrend in my universe. (8) BTC ~$63.9k, stabilising after a 21-month low near $58k, total crypto cap -48% from peak, driven by the Fed and ETF outflows — downtrend intact but a bounce is in progress. (9) XLF made a record high $56.18 (+8.7% in three months) — trend intact, but it is the highest equity-beta and credit-cycle-sensitive long I own into a hiking Fed.

decisions.reason: The trend signals I built this book on were not just confirmed this week, they were re-fuelled by a genuine regime event on 29 Jul: a hawkish Fed hold with three dissents FOR A HIKE, long yields up, Brent +7% to $90+ on Hormuz. That single catalyst simultaneously strengthens my dollar long (widening Fed/ECB gap), my precious-metals shorts (rising real yields is THE gold driver, and OCBC/consensus now sees further declines), my energy long (Hormuz supply constraint is what turned the Fed hawkish in the first place), my defensive healthcare long (XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul at +2.33% while the index fell 1.5%), and my consumer-discretionary short (4.2% CPI plus an energy shock plus hike risk is a direct squeeze on discretionary spend). So this is not a rebuild, it is a conviction-weighted resize of the same eleven trends, which is exactly what the new sizing freedom is for. Three changes. FIRST, I EXIT IWM ENTIRELY. It was already my weakest signal (only 0.1% above its 50dma, i.e. the fast trend had gone flat while the slow one was still up), and the 29 Jul event is precisely the catalyst that breaks it: BofA puts the damage at ~2% of R2K operating earnings per 25bp, small caps carry the most floating-rate debt and refi need, and a hike-biased Fed favours large balance sheets. Weekly reassessment is my real trend-exit mechanism and this is what it is for - I do not wait for a -20% catastrophe stop to tell me a trend has rolled. SECOND, I lift the four legs where the macro driver and the price trend now point the same way and the volatility is low enough to justify size: EUO 14 to 19 (lowest vol in the book at 9.9%, cleanest macro trend, inverse-vol sizing makes it the top weight on merit not on hunch), XLE 9 to 15 (best-established MA trend among the low-vol-enough names, 15.5% above its 200dma, with a live and re-accelerating supply catalyst), GLD short 6 to 10 and XLY short 8 to 10. XLV goes 13 to 14 and URA short 2 to 3 - URA is down 18% in a month and 10% in a week even with spot uranium firm at $86, the sharpest active downtrend I can find, capped only by its 51.8% vol. THIRD, I trim XLF 16 to 10. The trend is genuinely intact (record high $56.18, +8.7% in three months) so I am not exiting, but it is my highest equity-beta and most credit-cycle-exposed long and a hiking Fed is not its friend; that capital works harder in the dollar and energy legs. USO goes 3 to 5 but no further - 38% above its 200dma against 3m momentum of only +1.5% is the definition of an extended trend where the two filters disagree, and 51.7% vol plus whipsaw risk on any Hormuz diplomacy headline (oil fell three straight days to $79 before the 29 Jul spike) keeps it small with a -40% stop. I am NOT going to a one-line book. My mandate is time-series trend across six asset classes sized inversely to realised volatility, and the whole edge is that the equity, FX, commodity, metals and crypto sleeves each contribute similar risk from independent drivers - collapsing that into one name would be abandoning the strategy, not expressing conviction in it. Gross equity 94% keeps me inside the no-margin cap, cash 3% earns 4%, and the turnover here is a handful of basis points on maybe 30% of the book.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so the overlap rule does not bind; nonetheless this book is materially reshaped versus my 27 Jul Round-3 book - IWM is fully exited, XLF is cut by more than a third, and EUO, XLE, GLD-short, XLY-short, USO and URA-short are all materially resized around the 29 Jul hawkish-hold and Hormuz shock.

decisions.research_notes: Searched/fetched live market data on 2026-07-29/30. decisions.reason:
The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

Energy equities are still discounting crude far below spot after five months of a shut Strait of Hormuz, which gives me both the convergence upside and the downside cushion (2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x — equities cannot hand back a move they never made). Healthcare — the ballast that makes the energy concentration carryable. -0.07 correlation to XLE and 0.22 to SPY at only 13.7% annualised vol, +25.0% total return over the past year, re-rating off a multi-year derating base. The funding short and the cleanest statement of the thesis: an oil shock is a consumer tax, and Brent at $89 with Hormuz shut is a large one. Raised from 13% because it now does double duty — 23.2% AMZN plus 15.7% TSLA means 39% of this ETF sits at the intersection of the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that dragged XLK down 6.81% in July. Refining/crack-spread leg, sized up into the 4 August print — the only near-dated catalyst in the book. Consensus Q2 EPS of ~$11-12 is +184-199% y/y on ~$42bn revenue, with management having front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run 2.99mb/d at ~94% utilisation into this window. The $301.59 average price target is stale and sits below the $308.72 spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Cracks are a distinct driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not simply more ERX. Sized at 16% with a -25% stop, which caps single-name earnings-gap damage at 4.0% of NAV.

Small convexity leg on an engine asymmetry that still holds: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage x 10% APR, so the leverage here is free. DOGE is $0.0702, down 0.6% on the day, still pinned at the bottom of its range with no participation in any crypto bounce — the worst cross-sectional performer in the asset class. THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION — DISPERSION, NOT INDEX VOL: MSFT and META both reported the night of 29-Jul and moved in OPPOSITE directions by 16 points. MSFT beat ($4.74 vs $4.24, Azure +43%, past $100bn ARR, and cut CY26 capex guide from $190bn to $175bn by extending datacentre life to 25 years) and is +8.83% after hours. META missed ($6.18 vs $7.22 consensus, Reality Labs -$4.6bn, capex raised to $130-145bn) and is -7.45% after hours. Weighting those in SPY (~4.5% and ~2.5%) they net to roughly +0.2% of index — single-stock variance is exploding while index variance is mechanically damped by offsetting constituents. That is the textbook falling-implied-correlation regime my mandate is built on, and it is now confirmed violently rather than merely inferred. AAPL and AMZN both report 30-Jul after the close, so the dispersion event has another leg tonight; NVDA is 26-Aug. Also picked up sell-side commentary that "low-volatility stocks are having a moment after a long stretch of underperformance," i.e. the factor rotation is early rather than exhausted.

HONEST NEGATIVE FINDING ON MY OWN BOOK: I re-ran the arithmetic on the TQQQ/SQQQ decay pair against my own recorded backtest (mean +0.29% of notional per 63 sessions = ~1.2%/yr) and it does NOT clear the 3% APR short borrow on both legs. Even grossing the decay up for the fact that QQQ realized vol is running at the 80th percentile (decay scales with sigma-squared, so maybe 2x the historical mean) it only gets to roughly break-even, against a backtested worst 63-day of -27.76% of notional. That is variance with no expected return, so the leg gets cut hard rather than upsized — which is the opposite of what "high vol in the tech complex" naively suggested.

decisions.reason: The regime call is confirmed but its two halves have moved in opposite directions, so the book has to be re-weighted rather than held. CONFIRMED: dispersion is exploding. USMV fell 0.21% and SPLV 0.55% on a day SPY fell 1.54% and SMH fell 4.79%, and MSFT (+8.8%) and META (-7.5%) gapped 16 points apart after hours on the same night. That is exactly the falling-implied-correlation state I sized for, and the low-vol cross-section is absorbing almost none of the stress. So I lean into it: low-vol core goes 60% to 74% (USMV 36 to 44, SPLV 24 to 30), the highest-conviction and best-evidenced leg in the book. CHANGED: index implied vol is no longer at the 34th percentile — VIX is 20.66 and rising 13.5% in a day with AAPL and AMZN reporting tonight. Short index vol into a rising VIX with a live catalyst chain is the wrong side of the timing even though the variance risk premium is nominally wider (20.66 implied vs ~13-14% realized), so SVXY is halved 12% to 6% and its stop tightened from -25% to -20%. REFUTED BY MY OWN NUMBERS: the TQQQ/SQQQ short-gamma pair does not clear its financing. My recorded backtest mean is +0.29% of notional per 63 sessions (~1.2%/yr) against 3% APR borrow on each leg; even doubling the decay for 80th-percentile QQQ vol it is roughly break-even with a -27.76% worst-case tail. I cut it 10+10 to 7+7 rather than upsizing it, and redeploy the freed budget into the low-vol core where the expected return is actually positive. VIXY trims 5% to 4% and its take-profit drops from +90% to +50%: from an already-elevated VIX 20.66 base a +90% move needs a 2024-style event, whereas +50% (VIXY ~$34, VIX high-20s) is a spike I can realistically monetise into cash. decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book (my packet lists Round 3 only), so the <50% overlap constraint does not bind here; nonetheless this book is materially re-weighted from its predecessor, moving the low-vol core from 60% to 74%, halving SVXY, and cutting the leveraged-ETF decay pair by 30% after finding it fails to clear its borrow cost.

positions.thesis: Min-volatility equity core, upsized from 36% because it is the single best-confirmed leg in the book. Second low-vol sleeve, raised from 24%. Its value here is construction diversity from USMV: SPLV is a pure S&P-500 low-vol screen whose top holdings are Loews, FirstEnergy and J&J, giving it essentially zero semiconductor exposure at the exact moment the tape's stress is 'chip worries spreading' and Morgan Stanley is calling a hard remainder of 2026 for semis. Fell 0.55% on a SPY -1.54% day, 36% downside capture. Yields 2.09% vs USMV's 1.47%, so it also pays me to wait. Kept smaller than USMV because its 20d realized vol of 14.88% is meaningfully higher, and the vol-target rule tilts the core toward the lower-vol construction. Stop kept wider at 16% to match that higher vol.

Short-gamma leg, cut from 10% after an honest re-check of its economics. The leveraged-ETF compounding decay is real and running fast — TQQQ fell 6.19% on a QQQ -2.04% day, worse than a naive 3x, and QQQ realized vol at the 80th percentile accelerates the drag since decay scales with sigma-squared. But my own backtest mean of +0.29% of notional per 63 sessions annualises to ~1.2%, which does not clear the 3% APR borrow on each leg, against a worst 63-day of -27.76% of notional. So this is roughly a break-even carry with a fat left tail and it gets sized down, not up. It stays in the book at reduced size because it is the only leg that is long realized vol in the Nasdaq complex without taking directional risk, which is the regime call itself. Deliberately carries NO stop: it is one half of a hedged pair and an individual stop converts the structure into a naked directional short at the worst possible moment.

Equal-notional opposite leg, cut from 10% alongside TQQQ. The pair proved its neutrality on 29-Jul: TQQQ -6.19% and SQQQ +6.30% meant the equal-notional short lost only 0.11% of notional (about -0.01% of NAV) on one of the largest trend days of the quarter. Short TQQQ carries roughly -3 delta on QQQ and short SQQQ roughly +3, so P&L is the joint decay of both funds — a carry paid by chop and taxed by trend. At 7+7 the realistic bad case is around -3.9% of NAV versus -5.6% at the old sizing, which is the right price for a leg whose expected return is close to its financing cost. No individual stop, for the same structural reason as the TQQQ leg.

Variance-risk-premium harvest, halved from 12%. The premium is nominally WIDER than when I put the book on — VIX 20.66 against SPY realized of roughly 13-14% — and the dispersion regime structurally supports short INDEX vol, because offsetting mega-cap moves (MSFT +8.8%, META -7.5%) mechanically damp index realized even while single-stock variance explodes. That is the real mechanism and it argues for keeping the leg. But short vol into a VIX that just jumped 13.5% in a session, with AAPL and AMZN reporting tonight, NVDA on 26-Aug and an unresolved China-AI narrative, is the wrong entry timing: the first spike off a low base is often followed by a larger one. Halving the size and tightening the stop from -25% to -20% keeps the carry alive while capping the leg's contribution near -1.2% of NAV, versus -3% under the old sizing.

Convex left-tail hedge on a 74% low-vol equity core, trimmed from 5% and with the take-profit recalibrated from +90% to +50%. The trim reflects that the position already did its job — VIXY gained 6.07% on 29-Jul — and that buying more vol insurance after the pop, in a fund that bleeds 43.8% a year to contango, is paying up for a hedge post-event. The TP change is the more important edit: from an already-elevated VIX 20.66 base, a +90% move requires a 2024-style dislocation, whereas +50% (VIXY around $34, VIX in the high-20s to 30) is a genuine stress event I can realistically convert into cash rather than round-trip. No stop, because a stop on insurance defeats the purpose. This leg plus SVXY's reduced size is what lets me carry a 74% equity core with net portfolio beta near 0.45.
