decisions.name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
decisions.research_notes:
MACRO (29-30 Jul 2026): Warsh Fed held 9-3, read as hawkish; market now prices a possible SEPTEMBER HIKE. 30y Treasury at highest yield since 2007 — the bond market is openly doubting inflation containment and Warsh's credibility. Dow -1,000pts, worst Fed Day since Dec-2024. SPY -1.54% to $729 (only ~4% off its high) — so this is a RATE/MULTIPLE shock, not a growth shock, and it lands hardest on long-duration high-multiple equities.

AI-INFRA (the two overnight catalysts that reshaped my Round 2): MSFT after-hours +8.8% — Azure +41% and past $100B, but capex guided DOWN to $175B CY26 vs ~$190B expected, and datacenter useful life extended 15→25 years. META after-hours -7.5% — EPS $6.18 vs $7.22 est, capex RAISED to $130-145B. The market is now rewarding capex discipline and punishing capex expansion. That is a direct multiple headwind for undifferentiated capex beneficiaries. Damage already done: SMH $504 (-25% from $672 high, "chip stocks enter bear-market territory"), AMAT $436 (-41% from $740, fwd PE 29, DRAM/adv-packaging systems launched June, earnings Aug 13), VRT $223 (-17% IN ONE DAY on a sales miss $3.27B vs $3.38B, PE 50, -41% from high), MU $739 (-10% on the day, -41% from June peak, PE 18.5 / FWD PE 5.7), AVGO $370 (PE 63, Samsung $200B memory+foundry partnership; hyperscalers moving to custom accelerators), NVDA $190 (PE 29, -20% from high; memory costs flagged as a headwind for Vera Rubin), SMCI $25.70 (-9.7%, -59% from high, illegal-server-export-to-China probe, prelim Q4 "strong orders" caused a +24% squeeze earlier in the week, earnings Aug 11). GEV $900: decisive Q2 beat-and-raise, guidance +$1B, PE 25.8, avg PT $1,233 — yet the stock still fell 4.6%, i.e. good numbers are not being paid for right now. Key synthesis: electricity cannot be depreciated away by an accounting change, and memory is a genuine physical shortage inflating everyone else's bill of materials.

ROTATION BASKET (Round 3): XLE $58.65 UP 1.88% on a -1.54% SPY day, +37% 1yr — energy is outperforming on geopolitical supply fear, high oil and AI power demand; PE 21, 2.6% yield, beta 0.44. GLD $371 (gold ~$4,000/oz) rose +0.46% and +0.92% after-hours ON the hawkish Fed day — the debasement/credibility trade is waking up; GDX $73.57 is -37% from its $117 high at PE 13.6, a heavily levered call on that. COPX $76 +75% 1yr, -24% off high, AI buildout adding demand to materials. EWZ PE 9.8 / 4.1% yield but facing new 25-50% US tariffs on Brazilian goods. Critically, EEM is NOT a clean rotation vehicle: TSMC 15.2% + Samsung 6.2% + SK hynix 5.1% = ~26% semis, so it is a levered AI-semi proxy that both duplicates my Round 2 factor and contradicts the "rotate out of AI" mandate — it fell -2.07% today with the chips. UUP $28.42 sits near the TOP of its 52-week range ($26.40-$28.60) — with a hawkish Fed and hike risk, the short-dollar leg is fighting the tape.

decisions.reason: Two overnight catalysts hit this book directly and asymmetrically, so I am re-sizing within the mandate rather than defending the old mix. MSFT cutting CY26 capex to $175B (vs ~$190B expected) while extending datacenter useful life 15-to-25 years, and being rewarded +8.8% for it, while META is punished -7.5% for raising capex, tells me the market has switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE. Layer on a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk and 30y yields at 2007 highs, and undifferentiated high-multiple capex beneficiaries face a multiple headwind that good numbers will not fix (GEV beat, raised guidance $1B, and still fell 4.6%). So I cut broad beta and rack-capex exposure and concentrate into the three things this regime cannot depreciate away: (1) POWER - GEV to 22%, my highest-conviction leg, because electricity is a physical bottleneck, its backlog is contracted, PE 25.8 against a $1,233 average target, and its numbers just went UP; (2) SEMI-CAP - AMAT 16% at fwd PE 29 and -41% from its high, with the memory shortage forcing DRAM WFE spend and new DRAM/advanced-packaging systems shipping, earnings Aug 13; (3) THE MEMORY BOTTLENECK - new MU 12% at fwd PE 5.7 and -41% off the June peak, the purest picks-and-shovels in the stack now that rising memory cost is the thing flagged as constraining Vera Rubin. AVGO 13% because hyperscaler capex discipline is actively BULLISH for custom ASICs versus merchant GPUs, plus the $200B Samsung memory/foundry tie-up. ANET 8% kept as the cheaper, more durable networking leg. CUT ENTIRELY: VRT (sales miss, -17% in a day, PE 50, most exposed to hyperscaler efficiency gains), ALAB (highest multiple, no earnings support), NVT (indistinct), and SMH (broad beta that is 21% NVDA, which faces both memory-cost inflation and custom-silicon substitution - I want the specific names, not the index). On the leverage kicker: free sizing means I can size it at ZERO, and a 3x semis position into a hawkish Fed with chips in a bear market is the single worst risk/reward on the board, so there is none. The laggard short goes 5%-to-9% on SMCI, the exact loser of memory inflation - a ~10%-gross-margin assembler whose input cost is exploding, with an illegal-export probe running into Aug 11 earnings - but not larger, because it is already -59% from its high and squeezed +24% this week. Gross drops 90%-to-80% with 20% cash earning 4% APY, which is genuine optionality when the long end is at 2007 highs. Stops are deliberately WIDE (-22% to -28%) as catastrophe insurance only: single names moved 8-17% in one session today and any tight stop would simply be shredded at the low.

positions.thesis: GE Vernova: the power-generation bottleneck. Decisive Q2 beat-and-raise with guidance lifted $1B, PE 25.8, avg target $1,233 vs $900 spot. Unlike servers and GPUs, turbines and grid gear cannot be conjured away by extending depreciation schedules - electricity demand is electricity demand. Highest-conviction leg, doubled in weight.

Semi-cap equipment at fwd PE 29 and -41% from its $740 high. The memory shortage that is inflating everyone's bill of materials forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend; AMAT shipped new DRAM and advanced AI packaging systems in June. Earnings Aug 13 is a near-term catalyst into a washed-out price.

Custom AI silicon and networking. Hyperscaler capex discipline is a tailwind, not a headwind, for custom ASICs - they are the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer to MSFT's efficiency push. The ~$200B Samsung memory/foundry partnership through 2030 locks in supply. -25% from its high.

NEW. Memory is the actual physical shortage in the AI stack right now - rising memory cost is what analysts flag as the constraint on Vera Rubin systems, which means MU has the pricing power everyone else is paying for. PE 18.5, fwd PE 5.7, -41% from the June peak. Sized 12% not more because memory cyclicals always look cheapest near the top and ChangXin's Chinese DRAM debut is a real competitive event.
Arista back-end datacenter switching: durable AI networking demand at a materially lower multiple than the thermal/rack names I am cutting. Retained as the diversifying compute-fabric leg.

Increased 5%-to-9%. The precise loser of memory-cost inflation: a low-gross-margin server assembler whose largest input cost is exploding while its customers demand price discipline. Add an active illegal-server-export-to-China probe and Aug 11 earnings. Capped at 9% with a hard stop because it is already -59% from its high and squeezed +24% this week on a prelim orders update.

decisions.reason: The macro resolved decisively in favour of two legs of this mandate and against two others, so I am re-weighting hard rather than holding a book that is flat because its winners and losers are cancelling out. FOR: energy and gold. XLE rose +1.88% on a day SPY fell -1.54% and is +37% over the year on geopolitical supply fear, high oil and AI power demand - it is the real-asset carry leg working exactly as intended, so it goes to 26%. And gold ROSE (+0.46%, +0.92% after-hours, ~$4,000/oz) on the most hawkish Fed day since 2024 - that is the tell. When 30y yields hit 2007 highs specifically because the bond market doubts the Fed can contain inflation and Warsh's credibility is being openly questioned, that IS the gold thesis, and GDX at PE 13.6 and -37% from its high is the levered expression of it, so 22%. I am also REMOVING the +40% take-profit on GDX: I do not want to be automatically forced out of my best macro leg right as it starts working. AGAINST: the dollar short and EEM. UUP sits near the TOP of its 52-week range with a hawkish Fed and September hike risk - the near-term rate differential is against me even though the long-run credibility story is not - so the dollar short is cut 8%-to-3%, kept only as the token leg the mandate calls for. EEM is CUT ENTIRELY: its top three holdings are TSMC 15.2%, Samsung 6.2% and SK hynix 5.1%, roughly a quarter of the fund in semis, which makes it a levered AI-chip proxy dressed as emerging markets. Owning it both contradicts the 'rotate out of US mega-cap AI' mandate and doubles down on the exact factor my Round 2 book already carries; it fell -2.07% today with the chips. Its weight goes to energy and gold. COPX 12% retained as the commodity/electrification leg (+75% 1yr, -24% off high). EWZ trimmed 12%-to-10% purely on the new 25-50% US tariffs on Brazilian goods, though PE 9.8 and a 4.1% yield still make it the cheapest carry available. EZU 10% and EWJ 9% held as the non-US, non-AI value legs, with the BOJ meeting live for EWJ. Stops widened across the board (-18% to -22%) so the thesis has room in a high-volatility rate regime instead of being whipsawed out at the low.
decisions.novelty: Zero symbol overlap and zero same-direction gross-weight overlap with my Round 2 book: Round 2 is US AI-infrastructure equity (GEV, AMAT, AVGO, MU, ANET long, SMCI short), while Round 3 is entirely real assets and ex-US value (XLE, GDX, COPX, EWZ, EZU, EWJ long, UUP short) - and I deliberately cut EEM this round precisely because its ~26% semiconductor weighting was the one place the two books were quietly converging on the same AI factor.

positions.thesis: Energy carry, now the anchor leg. Up +1.88% on a -1.54% SPY day and +37% over the year on geopolitical supply fear, elevated oil and AI-driven power demand. PE 21, 2.6% yield, beta 0.44 - real-asset cash flow is exactly what outperforms when the bond market is repricing inflation risk.

Gold miners as the levered Fed-credibility trade. Gold rose on the hawkish Fed day and holds ~$4,000/oz while 30y yields hit 2007 highs on doubts the Fed can contain inflation. Miners at PE 13.6 and -37% from their high are earning enormous margins at this gold price. Take-profit REMOVED so I am not forced out of the thesis early; stop widened to -20%.

Copper miners: tight physical supply meeting electrification and datacenter buildout demand. +75% over the past year and still -24% below its high, with a 2.5% yield. The commodity-linked real-asset leg of the rotation.

Brazil at PE 9.8 with a 4.1% dividend yield - the highest real-rate carry and cheapest valuation in the basket, with commodity leverage via Vale. Trimmed from 12% only because of newly imposed 25-50% US tariffs on Brazilian exports.
Eurozone value re-rating on ECB easing plus sustained fiscal and defense spending. Non-US, non-AI earnings stream with no exposure to the hyperscaler capex debate.
Japan corporate-governance reform and buyback story, low correlation to US tech. BOJ forward guidance at its two-day meeting is the live catalyst; a firmer yen would add to dollar-based returns.

Cut 8%-to-3%. Kept as the token dollar short the mandate requires, but heavily reduced: UUP sits near the top of its 52-week range and a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk means the near-term rate differential favours the dollar, even if the fiscal-credibility story eventually does not.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum
decisions.research_notes:
WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I pulled fresh daily bars myself from the Yahoo chart API (last equity close 2026-07-29, crypto live 07-30) for ~130 ETFs/stocks, computed 1w/2w/1m/3m/6m trend plus performance since each book was set, then read news via the Yahoo news endpoints and WebFetch.

REGIME: a violent AI-capex unwind. SOXX -16.3% 1w / -24.3% 1m; SMH -14.1/-20.2; semi-cap destroyed (AMAT -21/-37, LRCX -21/-39, KLAC -21/-39, MU -23/-35, ASML -14/-18, ALAB -25/-45, VRT -26/-27). SOXL -42.9% in ONE week, -61% 1m. MTUM (the momentum factor ETF itself) -9.9% 1w / -15.7% 1m: a textbook crowded-momentum crash, not a dip.

CATALYSTS CONFIRMED: (1) Meta 07-29/30 - revenue beat $60.8bn but EPS missed 14%, costs +55%, FREE CASH FLOW COLLAPSED 91% to $784m, FY capex guided to $130-145bn; stock -10%, framed as "a broader earnings-season pattern in which AI infrastructure spending is unsettling investors." The market has flipped the sign on capex: spending is now punished. (2) Fed held with THREE dissents; Chair Kevin Warsh's comments "sent the stock market tumbling"; "Dow sees worst day in over a year, Nasdaq enters correction territory." VIX 20.66, +13.5%. (3) AI CREDIT cracking - Burry flags NVDA 5Y CDS parabolic; Oracle default insurance hit 200bp at a 52-week low. (4) Qualcomm tepid guide; Japan earthquake hit TSMC/Toyota ops; Kospi selloff; "$2 trillion AI rout."

WHERE MONEY IS GOING (positive 1w AND 1m AND 3m): Healthcare cleanest - XLV +4.3/+3.4/+16.1 (ABT +7.4/+17.3, TMO +9.5/+13.8, HCA +9.8, AMGN +5.9/+7.5, ABBV 3m +34, LLY 3m +39). Staples XLP +3.5/+3.5/+5.9 (KO +8.4/+7.8/+14.4, PM 3m +21, KMB 3m +17). Defense post-earnings drift: RTX +10.5/+14.9/+23.0, LMT +10.7/+13.4/+11.8. Energy strongest 1m sector: XLE +9.5% 1m / +19.7% 6m (XOM +15.2% 1m). Telecom carry VZ +6.6/+8.9/+24.0 6m, T +3.9/+11.2. Low-vol USMV +2.2/+2.3/+5.2, SPLV +1.8/+2.8/+5.2; XLRE +2.1/+2.3/+13.2 6m. AAPL is the best large-cap trend in the universe (+3.8/+20.0/+25.0/+31.2, just crossed $5tn) precisely because it is the anti-capex tech name - but it reports tonight (07-30), so I sized it modestly rather than heroically.

CLEANEST SHORTS (negative on EVERY horizon = true time-series momentum, not a stretched short): ORCL -6.4/-20.0/-28.8/-32.2 with CDS 200bp and Ellison backstopping $40.4bn of a media deal; TSLA -20.2/-27.6/-20.7/-30.8, worst week since 2022 as investors balked at robotaxi/AI spending. Semis (SOXX/SOXL) are still positive on 3m/6m, so I sized that leg smaller and stopped it - that is where squeeze risk lives.

CRYPTO: my original short-crypto sleeve has lost its edge. BTC 1m now +2.6%, ETH +9.7% 1m / +2.8% 1w; only SOL still trends down. The persistent BTC/ETH downtrend has flattened, so I will not pay borrow and slippage to re-express it.

RATES/GOLD for the carry book: duration is not being paid - TLT -4.9% 1m, IEF -1.7% 1m, hawkish Fed with three dissents. XLU (-2.2/-2.4) is no longer a clean bond proxy: it is contaminated by the AI-datacenter-power narrative now unwinding (SRE -5.4% 1m, AEP -6.2%). GDX -16.9% 3m / -32.7% 6m is a broken trend, not convexity. Cash at 4% APY is a genuinely competitive carry asset with zero drawdown.

decisions.reason: Momentum means following the trend that exists, not the trend I wish existed - and the trend has inverted hard. The AI-capex complex broke on real, dated catalysts (Meta's FCF -91% on a $130-145bn capex guide, Oracle CDS at 200bp, NVDA CDS parabolic, Qualcomm's miss, a hawkish Fed with three dissents, VIX 20.66). MTUM itself is -15.7% in a month, which is the signature of a crowded-momentum unwind: the correct trend-following response is to rotate to the new leaders and short the former ones, never to buy the fallen leaders back. So I keep every piece of my mandate's machinery - directional equity momentum, a funding short sleeve, weekly reassessment, a cash buffer - and let the sign flip where the data says it flipped. The long side is the only group positive on 1w AND 1m AND 3m simultaneously: healthcare (XLV +4.3/+3.4/+16.1), staples, defense on post-earnings drift (RTX +10.5% 1w, LMT +10.7% 1w), energy (strongest 1m sector), telecom carry (VZ), and AAPL, the anti-capex tech leader and best large-cap trend in my universe. I cut AAPL to 9% rather than 15% purely because it reports tonight and I refuse a gap risk I am not paid for. The funding sleeve is no longer short crypto - BTC 1m is now +2.6% and ETH +9.7%, so that downtrend has flattened and I will not pay costs to chase a dead signal - it is short the broken AI-capex complex instead, which is the same trade my mandate always described, just on the other side of the sign. ORCL and TSLA are negative on all four horizons with no positive-momentum leg at all, exactly what a time-series momentum short wants; the semis leg is smaller and stopped because SOXX is still +6% on 3m and +33% on 6m, so that is where squeeze risk lives, and SOXL adds 3x short beta plus volatility decay from only 4% of capital. Net beta lands near 0.15, deliberately: with a hawkish Fed, rising VIX and AI credit stress I want return from the long/short spread (XLV +4.3% vs SOXX -16.3% in one week) rather than market direction. I am not forcing 3x long ETFs to satisfy the word 'leveraged' - buying TQQQ or SOXL long into a momentum crash would be the single most destructive thing I could do here.

positions.thesis: The only sector positive on 1w, 1m, 3m and 6m at once (+4.3/+3.4/+16.1/+7.9) with real breadth - ABT, TMO, HCA, AMGN, JNJ, ABBV, LLY, MRK all trending. Capital fleeing AI capex needs cash-flow-return defensives and this is where it is landing. Largest position because it is the highest-quality trend at the lowest volatility.
Staples +3.5% 1w / +3.5% 1m / +5.9% 3m with KO +8.4% 1w and PM, KMB, CL, MO all up on 3m. Low-beta dividend momentum that historically leads for months once a growth-crowding unwind begins.

+10.5% 1w, +14.9% 1m, +23.0% 3m on a post-earnings breakout. Post-earnings-announcement drift is the most reliable momentum anomaly there is, and defense budgets are indifferent to hyperscaler capex discipline.
+10.7% 1w, +13.4% 1m, +11.8% 3m on a fresh post-earnings move. Pairs with RTX as an uncorrelated-to-AI momentum sleeve with real backlog visibility.

Best large-cap trend in the universe (+3.8/+20.0/+25.0/+31.2, just crossed $5tn) and structurally the anti-capex tech name: it monetises AI on-device instead of building $130bn of data centres, so it wins the exact rotation killing the rest of tech. Sized 9% not 15% because Q3 earnings land tonight - strong iPhone 17 shipment data plus momentum is positive expectancy, but not worth a 15% gap.

Strongest 1m sector at +9.5%, +19.7% on 6m, XOM +15.2% 1m. Commodity momentum re-engaging gives a genuinely different return driver from the defensive equity sleeve, and it is the one long that benefits if the Fed's inflation worry proves right.
+6.6% 1w, +8.9% 1m, +24.0% 6m on a ~6% dividend. High-carry, low-beta trend with zero AI-capex exposure - the cleanest small diversifier available.

The core sign-flip of my own mandate: -16.3% 1w and -24.3% 1m as the market repriced AI capex, with semi-cap equipment (AMAT/LRCX/KLAC near -21% in a week, -38% in a month) leading down. Hyperscalers are trapped - cut capex and orders collapse, keep spending and their own stock gets hit like Meta's did. Stopped at 15% because 3m and 6m are still positive, so this is a 1m downtrend inside a longer uptrend and squeezes can be vicious.

The single cleanest trend short available: negative on 1w, 1m, 3m and 6m (-6.4/-20.0/-28.8/-32.2) with no positive-momentum leg at all. At a 52-week low with default insurance at 200bp and Ellison personally backstopping $40.4bn of a media deal - the most debt-funded AI-capex story in the market, being repriced by the credit market first.

Capital-efficient version of the same view: 3x short semis beta from only 4% of the book, plus volatility decay that bleeds the instrument even in violent sideways chop (SOXL -61% in a month against SOXX -24%). Stop and take-profit attached because a leveraged-ETF short is the one position here with genuinely unbounded upside risk.

Also negative on all four horizons (-20.2/-27.6/-20.7/-30.8) and its worst week since 2022 specifically because investors balked at Musk's robotaxi and AI spending plans - the identical capex-punishment theme. Kept to 3% only because it sits 3% above its 52-week low, which is where forced-cover squeezes start.

decisions.reason: The carry book has done its job - flat at +0.05% with a -0.75% max drawdown while the Nasdaq entered correction - but three of its four carry sleeves have stopped paying and I would rather fix them now than collect a coupon into a drawdown. First, duration is not being paid: TLT -4.9% on 1m and IEF -1.7%, with the Fed on hold against THREE dissents and Warsh talking hawkishly. Term premium is a thesis about being compensated for rate risk, and right now I take the risk without the compensation, so TLT goes entirely and IEF stays only as the genuine risk-off hedge if this AI unwind becomes a growth scare. Second, the insight I actually care about: XLU is no longer a bond proxy. It was quietly repriced over the past year as the AI-datacenter-power trade and is now unwinding with the rest of it - SRE -5.4% 1m, AEP -6.2%, XLU -2.4% 1m. Holding it as a 'defensive low-beta income' sleeve means holding hidden AI beta inside a book whose entire purpose is not to have any, so it goes and its income role passes to XLP, KO and T, which carry similar yield with actual positive momentum and no capex contamination. Third, GDX at -16.9% on 3m and -32.7% on 6m is not convexity, it is leverage pointed at a downtrending asset; I take the +4% bounce since the book was set and exit. I also cut SPY, because inverse-vol balancing says the equity risk premium should come from USMV and SPLV, up 2%+ on the week while SPY fell 2.4%. HYG comes from 15 to 11 with a tight stop: high yield still pays its ~7% coupon, but with NVDA's CDS parabolic and Oracle's at 200bp the AI complex's debt is the fattest tail in credit and I want a defined exit rather than a thesis. What replaces all of it is carry that is actually working - XLRE rent yield, XLE energy FCF, KO and T dividend carry, all with positive multi-horizon trend - plus 8% cash, which at 4% APY with zero drawdown is a legitimately competitive carry asset when both duration and credit are impaired. Net beta stays low, the basket stays inverse-vol weighted with the lowest-volatility sleeves carrying the largest weights, and the mandate is unchanged: I harvest the carry that is being paid instead of the carry that used to be.
decisions.novelty: This book shares only 15 points of same-direction gross weight with my Round-2 book (XLP 8 and XLE 7, about 16% of gross, far under the 50% limit): Round 2 is a concentrated long/short momentum spread that is short 18% of semis, Oracle and Tesla and long single-name trend leaders (AAPL, RTX, LMT, XLV, VZ), while Round 3 holds none of those, runs no shorts at all, and is built from instruments Round 2 does not touch - USMV, SPLV, IEF, HYG, GLD, XLRE, KO and T - as a long-only inverse-vol cross-asset carry basket.

positions.thesis: Min-volatility equity is the core equity-risk-premium sleeve and it is earning its keep: +2.2% 1w and +2.3% 1m while SPY fell 2.4% on the week. Lowest volatility in the basket, so inverse-vol weighting hands it the largest allocation.

7-10y Treasuries are the only asset here that rallies if the AI capex unwind turns into a growth scare, and 1w has already stabilised at +0.1%. Term premium is thin with a hawkish Fed, so I hold the intermediate belly for the hedge and refuse the long end entirely.

Credit-spread carry at roughly a 7% yield remains the book's income engine and spreads have not actually widened yet (3m flat). Cut from 15 to 11 and stopped tightly at -6% because the AI complex is debt-funded and its credit is where stress is appearing first - NVDA CDS parabolic, Oracle at 200bp.

Gold stays as the low-correlation real-asset diversifier and best hedge against the AI-credit tail, and its 1m has turned marginally positive (+0.7%) after a rough quarter. Trimmed rather than cut because a hawkish Fed and rising real rates are a genuine headwind - I want the insurance, not a directional bet.

Low-volatility equity alongside USMV: +1.8% 1w, +2.8% 1m, +5.2% 3m. Different construction from USMV (pure realised-vol screen versus optimised), so it diversifies the sleeve while keeping portfolio variance down.

Consumer staples as the defensive dividend-carry sleeve, +3.5% on both 1w and 1m. Takes over the bond-proxy income role from utilities with similar yield, similar beta and none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure.
REITs harvest rent carry and are quietly working: +2.1% 1w, +2.3% 1m, +13.2% 6m. A distinct cash-flow stream from both equities and credit, which is exactly what a cross-asset carry book should own.

Energy is the strongest 1m sector at +9.5% with +19.7% on 6m and pays real dividend and FCF carry. It is also the book's only inflation-linked leg, which matters given the Fed's own three dissenters are worried about exactly that.
+8.4% 1w, +7.8% 1m, +14.4% 3m, +22.7% 6m on a stable dividend. Defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple - the single-name expression of where low-beta money is actually going.

Telecom yield carry with momentum: +3.9% 1w and +11.2% 1m on a high dividend. Regulated domestic cash flows with essentially no correlation to the AI capex cycle driving every other risk asset right now.

decisions.name: Opus Quality Defensive
decisions.research_notes:
Pulled full price/trend history (1d/5d/1m/3m/6m/12m plus 50d & 200d moving-average position) for ~60 tickers via Yahoo chart data through the 2026-07-29 close. WebSearch budget was exhausted and most news sites returned 503/403, so the read is built from price action, which was unusually unambiguous.

REGIME: a memory/foundry capex bust plus a rates-and-oil inflation impulse — NOT a broad crash. MU -35.5% 1m, INTC -37.8%, AMD -20.4%, TSM -17.7%, SMH -20.2% (-14.1% in 5 days, -4.8% on 7/29). But NVDA only -2.5% 1m, AVGO -0.6%, MSFT +6.0%, AAPL +20.0%, META +4.1% — the damage is concentrated in the capex/memory complex, not AI compute leaders. SPY just -1.6% 1m, equal-weight RSP +1.3% 1m and +6.0% 3m, HYG -1.0% (no credit stress). VIX 20.7, +24% on the week. This is a rotation out of one crowded trade, not a systemic event.

WHERE MONEY IS GOING: healthcare is the decisive leader and it is broad, not one name — XLV +13.9% 3m/+23.9% 12m, VHT +14.3% 3m, LLY +29.5%, ABBV +24.6%, MRK +19.4%, JNJ +15.5%, UNH +13.5%, IBB +11.8%, PPH +11.4%, IHI +7.9% in 5d. XLV sits +6.8% over its 50d and +9.2% over its 200d. Also bid: staples (XLP +3.5% 1m, KO +7.8% 1m/+13.1% 3m), dividend-quality (SCHD +6.0% 1m, +15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m, +12.4% over 200d), energy (XLE +9.5% 1m, +18.1% 6m), financials (+5.5% 1m).

TWO KEY NEGATIVE FINDINGS THAT CHANGED MY BOOKS:
1) QUAL is the wrong quality vehicle. MSCI USA Quality is heavy in exactly the megacaps de-rating: -0.6% 1m versus XLV +3.4% and SCHD +6.0%. It delivered tech beta, not defense. SCHD's ROE/FCF-and-leverage screen is the same quality factor without the AI-bubble exposure and it beats QUAL on every horizon.
2) Gold is broken, and so are bonds. GLD -22.1% 6m, -4.1% below its 50d and -9.9% below its 200d; GDX -16.7% 3m, SLV -22.3%. The +2.7% gold pop on 7/29 is a bounce inside a confirmed downtrend. TLT is -5.3% 1m with 10y yields at 4.62% and rising. With both traditional hedges failing, cash at 4% APY is genuinely the superior non-equity ballast, so I zeroed the gold diversifier rather than keep hedging theater.

ON THE SMH SHORT (held in both books): the trend is my best idea, but SMH is now -15.5% below its 50-day while still +12.4% ABOVE its 200-day and +70% over 12 months. That is a violent correction inside a long-term uptrend, stretched and squeeze-prone. So I let it run at roughly existing size with stops attached, and deliberately did NOT add into the capitulation.

CRYPTO (Round 3): the trend filter says no. BTC -26.0% 12m, -10.1% 6m, -10.6% below its 200d. ETH -32.4% 12m, -11.7% 6m, -9.7% below its 200d — though ETH is +8.6% above its 50d and +10.0% 1m, the strongest short-term crypto momentum. Both majors below their 200-day means a trend-stacking mandate must cut, not hold. Also cut MTUM entirely (-15.7% 1m, -10.5% below its 50d) and cut JEPI hard — it is -2.9% over 6m, +0.1% over 12m and below its 200-day, i.e. dead money that only earns its keep as the option-carry mandate leg. Commodity/energy carry is the one genuinely confirmed, accelerating uptrend: PDBC +20.2% 6m/+30.2% 12m and +12.6% over its 200d, XLE +18.1% 6m/+33.8% 12m.

decisions.reason: The tape is validating this mandate precisely — capital is rotating out of the AI-capex complex into cheap defensive cash-flow — so the fix is not to change the strategy but to stop diluting it. Three changes. (1) XLV 19% to 36%: healthcare is the single highest-conviction idea available to a defensive book right now, leading on 1m (+3.4%), 3m (+13.9%) and 12m (+23.9%), above both its 50- and 200-day, and broad across LLY/ABBV/MRK/JNJ/UNH/IBB rather than resting on one name. Free sizing exists for exactly this. (2) QUAL 18% to zero, replaced by SCHD 16%: QUAL is ~30% technology and returned -0.6% over the month while the defensives it was supposed to sit beside made money — it was selling me tech beta under a quality label. SCHD applies a return-on-capital and FCF/leverage screen without the AI-bubble exposure and beat it on every horizon (+15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m). This keeps the quality-factor leg of the mandate and fixes the vehicle. (3) GLD 6% to zero and SPLV 11% folded into USMV. Gold is -22% over six months and below both moving averages; with TLT also -5.3% on the month, both traditional hedges have failed, and cash at 4% APY is the honest defensive ballast. SPLV and USMV are near-duplicate min-vol exposures, and SPLV's utilities tilt is a liability with yields rising (XLU -2.4% 1m), so I consolidated into the better-diversified one. I am holding the SMH short at 8% rather than pressing it: it has done its job, but SMH is 15% below its 50-day while still 12% above its 200-day, and adding to a short after a -20% month is how you get squeezed. Stops go on the short only — a defensive mandate must not stop out of its defensives into a drawdown. Turnover is ~60% at ~2bps/side, roughly 2.4bps of NAV, trivially worth it.

positions.thesis: The conviction position. Healthcare leads on every horizon (+3.4% 1m, +13.9% 3m, +23.9% 12m), trades above its 50d and 200d, is the cheapest large defensive sector, and the leadership is broad across pharma, managed care, biotech and devices rather than a single name. In a rotation from expensive long-duration tech into cheap cash-flow, this is the biggest and best-quality destination — so I am sizing it like a real view instead of a diversification slot.

Replaces QUAL as the quality-factor sleeve. Same factor — screens on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage — but without the ~30% technology weight that made QUAL a de-rating megacap proxy (-0.6% 1m). SCHD returned +6.0% 1m, +15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m and sits 12.4% above its 200-day. Quality that is actually defensive.

Min-vol core ballast, now carrying the whole low-volatility allocation after folding in the redundant SPLV sleeve. +2.3% 1m and above both moving averages. Preferred over SPLV because SPLV's heavy utilities tilt is a headwind with 10-year yields at 4.62% and rising (XLU -2.4% 1m).

Consumer staples: low-beta cash-flow ballast that is participating, not just defending (+3.5% 1m, above 50d and 200d). KO +7.8% 1m and +13.1% 3m, COST +5.0% and WMT +4.5% over five days as the rotation reaches the group.

The AI-infra overextension view, still sized as insurance rather than a bet. It has worked hard (SMH -20.2% 1m, -14.1% in five days) as the memory and foundry complex broke — MU -35%, INTC -38%, AMD -20%, TSM -18%. I am deliberately not adding: SMH is 15% below its 50-day but still 12% above its 200-day and +70% over twelve months, so this is a stretched correction inside a long-term uptrend and squeeze risk is real. Stop caps a squeeze, take-profit banks the gain if the bust extends.

decisions.reason: This is a trend-stacking mandate, so I applied the trend filter honestly and it told me to sell most of what I own. Cuts: MTUM to zero (-15.7% 1m, -9.9% in five days, 10.5% below its 50-day — the momentum factor IS the crowded AI trade that is unwinding, and a trend book cannot be long the worst-trending factor). BTC 16% to 5% and ETH 9% to 6% — both majors are below their 200-day (BTC -26% 12m, ETH -32% 12m), and a trend mandate follows the trend even when the trend is in its headline sleeve; ETH keeps the larger stub only because it is +8.6% above its 50-day with the strongest short-term crypto momentum. JEPI 16% to 8% — it returned +0.1% over twelve months and sits below its 200-day, so it is dead money that survives only as the covered-call carry leg the mandate requires. Adds go into the one genuinely confirmed and accelerating trend in the market: commodity and energy carry. PDBC 14% to 24% (+10.9% 1m, +20.2% 6m, +30.2% 12m, 12.6% above its 200-day, with oil +18.5% on the month and a +5.8% day on 7/29). New XLE at 14% — the equity expression of the same supply shock, +9.5% 1m and +18.1% 6m, and it pays a dividend, so it is trend and carry in one line. DBMF stays 20% as the managed-futures core, positioned long commodities and short equities and bonds, which is exactly this tape. SMH short nudged 7% to 9% as the strongest downtrend available. Cash rises to 14% because there are not enough confirmed uptrends to fill the book, and forcing capital into assets below their 200-day to avoid holding cash would be the precise mistake this mandate exists to prevent — idle cash earns 4% APY. Managed-futures cross-asset trend, held as the mandate's core diversifier. This is the sleeve that gets structurally long the new downtrend without my having to pick each leg.

New position: the equity expression of the commodity trend, and trend plus carry in a single line. +9.5% 1m, +18.1% 6m, +33.8% 12m, above its 50-day and 11.8% above its 200-day, riding the same oil supply shock as PDBC while paying a healthy dividend yield. The strongest downtrend in the market and therefore a natural long for a trend book expressed as a short: SMH -20.2% 1m and -14.1% in five days, with the memory and foundry complex breaking outright (MU -35%, INTC -38%, AMD -20%, TSM -18%). decisions.reason: The rotation my mandate was built for has arrived and the evidence now separates my winners from my dead money cleanly. Confirmations: UNH beat Q2 by 31% and raised guidance with a $475 target vs $420 spot; CRM +3.79% and ADBE +5.72% on a day SPY fell 1.54%, with ADBE at 15x and CRM at 22x — the 'AI kills software' fear trade is visibly unwinding; XLV is being called a haven for investors ditching tech and State Street upgraded healthcare to positive. Meanwhile SOXL fell 16% in a single session on a genuinely structural catalyst (Chinese state-backed chips in mass production, AI-capex sustainability doubt) while still sitting on +242% YTD — my short is no longer just a leverage-decay valuation view, it has a fundamental driver. So I concentrate into the four validated value longs and roughly double the SOXL short. Against that, crypto is where my losses live and it has no catalyst: BTC is 49% off its high with ETF outflows, SOL is 75% off its high and still falling. I cut BTC in half, exit SOL entirely as a failed mean-reversion, and exit the BTC perp because paying 10% APR funding to be long a bleeding asset is a pure tax I no longer need now that sizing is free. I keep ETH at full weight because it is the one crypto actually mean-reverting (+17.6% over 30 days) with a real institutional catalyst. GLD stays as the hedge that has earned its place. Free sizing does not mean maximum sizing: my mandate explicitly warns that momentum-shorting is a portfolio killer, so the SOXL short goes to 15%, not 40%, with a 40% stop that caps the damage at roughly 6% of NAV if JPMorgan's buy-the-dip call proves right.

positions.thesis: Highest-conviction validated value long, raised 12->16%. Raised 7->11%. Up 5.72% in a single session, trading at 15.1x with revenue +11.5% and earnings +28%. It is the most extreme valuation dislocation I can find in profitable quality software, which is precisely the asymmetry my mandate exists to buy.

Cut 13->6%. Still the most resilient crypto and 49% off its high, so a residual oversold long remains consistent with the mandate, but persistent ETF outflows and a Fed on hold give it no near-term catalyst. It no longer deserves to be a top-three weight.

decisions.reason: This is the moment trend-following exists for, and the honest reading is that my momentum sleeve is not a momentum book at all — it is a semiconductor book. SPMO's top ten is 51% of assets led by Micron 10.3%, NVIDIA 8.2% and Broadcom 6.8%, and that complex just broke: SPMO -3.25% and XLK -2.64% on the day SOXL fell 16%. Trend discipline says you reduce a breaking leader rather than defend it, so SPMO goes 14->6%, XLK is exited entirely, and MTUM is exited as redundant semi-concentration. The corollary is that I must rotate to where relative strength actually is, and the tape told me: XLE rose 1.88% while SPY fell 1.54%, it has returned 37.3% over the past year with refiner margins at records and oil supported by US-Iran tensions, making it the strongest verified trend I can observe — it goes 8->16%. GOOGL rose 0.90% on the same red day at 16.7x with net income up 111%, which is the cleanest quality-momentum combination available and far less exposed to the hardware cycle now breaking, so it goes 8->13%. The quality and low-volatility ballast (QUAL, SCHD, JEPQ, SPLV) all step up, because a 16% single-day move in a 3x fund is a volatility-regime signal and these are the trend-compatible way to stay invested through it. AAPL is trimmed 8->6% with the stop tightened to 10% and the take-profit cut to 25%: it is a genuine leader near 52-week highs, but it reports tomorrow at 41x with a consensus target of $322 sitting below the $338 spot, which is a binary event with negative expected upside. Cash rises to 15% deliberately — trend-following with no confirmed signal means no position, and idle cash earns 4% while leadership re-forms.

Raised 10->12%. High return-on-equity, low-leverage balance sheets are historically the part of the trend complex that holds up best when high-beta leadership cracks, which is exactly the transition now underway. It keeps me inside my factor mandate while shedding the semiconductor beta that broke it.

Raised 9->10%. Option premium is richest precisely when realized volatility spikes the way it just did, so this sleeve's carry improves at the exact moment my directional sleeves are struggling. It is the most counter-cyclical income I can hold without leaving the mandate.

Raised 6->10%. A 16% single-day move in a 3x semiconductor fund is a volatility-regime signal, not noise, and low-volatility equity is the trend-compatible way to stay fully engaged with far less drawdown sensitivity than the high-beta sleeves I just cut.

Trimmed 8->6% with the stop tightened from 14% to 10% and the take-profit cut from 40% to 25%. Smaller size and a tight stop is how a trend follower owns a leader into a coin flip.

Cut hard from 14% to 6%. Its top ten is 51% of assets led by Micron 10.3%, NVIDIA 8.2% and Broadcom 6.8%, so it is currently a semiconductor bet wearing a momentum label, and it is already 16% below its 52-week high. decisions.reason: The book is working (+2.76% NAV, -0.45% max drawdown) but three positions deteriorated on hard news in the last 48 hours and two improved on beat-and-raise quarters, so I am resizing rather than rebuilding. CUTS: CAT to zero — a 31-year streak does not save a 0.83%-yielding AI-capex cyclical that fell 6.91% in a session on a Baird downgrade plus the New York data-center construction moratorium; it was the least mandate-true line I owned and the news confirmed it. TRIMS: PG 8 to 6 on the revenue miss, the 1-3% FY27 organic guide and the HSBC downgrade; JNJ 8 to 5 on the guidance cut to $10.86-11.01 and the $5.5B talc settlement, with only 1.9% to consensus; ADP 5 to 4 because a 17% EPS-growth quarter is excellent but the stock popped 3.48% straight through the $270 consensus target; MCD 6 to 3, half size into an Aug 3 print at a depressed price. ADDS: SCHD 18 to 33 — this is where my genuine conviction sits, and the new freedom lets me express it. It is the single cleanest instrument for this exact mandate at a 0.06% fee, 3.10% yield and 28.94% trailing return, and because it is a 103-stock quality basket a 33% weight carries almost no idiosyncratic or earnings-event risk; this is concentration into diversification, not variance for its own sake. KO 7 to 13, my largest single name, on a Jul 28 beat with 5% volume and 6% organic growth, RAISED FY guidance, a World Cup engagement tailwind and fresh $104 targets from UBS and Jefferies against $89.08. New CVX at 8% — a 38-year raiser yielding 3.71% at 11x forward earnings with $215 consensus, a better dividend-growth expression of the strongest sector than XOM alone. ABT 5 to 9 on the beat-and-raise and its habit of closing green on red days. ABBV held at 8 and XOM trimmed 7 into their Jul 31 prints, deliberately sized so that one shared earnings date does not dominate the book. Net effect: gross exposure unchanged at 96% with the mandated 4% cash sleeve earning 4% APY, but the staples/healthcare/quality-income core is denser, the cyclical and consumer-discretionary drift is gone, and turnover is cheap at roughly 2bps per side.

Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse). That is cheap catastrophe insurance on my largest line, not market timing. Turnover is real but this is one rebalance held to year-end, not churn.

KEY INFERENCES.

(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.

(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

WHAT I CUT AND WHY. XLF (12%->0): weakest momentum I own on every horizon, YTD +4.4% and 1yr +8.5% - a momentum book sells its laggard. TNA (8%->0): 3x small-cap beta with the 30-year at 2007 highs and three FOMC members dissenting for a HIKE is the single worst risk I could carry; 8% at 3x was 24% of effective exposure pointed straight into the headwind. IWM (7%->0) and IWD (10%->0): same rate-sensitivity, plus Wells Fargo flagging that small-cap gains mask falling earnings estimates. XBI 15%->7%: the mandate keeps me in biotech on its +71.6% 12-month trend, but it is 10.7% below its high and the healthcare rotation is flowing into large-cap pharma, not long-duration small-cap biotech. KRE 14%->10%: still 2.5% off its high and a steepener helps NIM, so it stays, but trimmed to fund conviction.

WHAT I BACKED. Energy goes from 15% to 54% nominal (~60% effective). It is the only theme in my scan that is simultaneously strong (+37.3% 1yr, +33% YTD), intact (7.6% off high) and accelerating - and it printed +1.88% on a day the Dow fell 1,000 points. The trend predates the Iran strike, so the supply shock is a catalyst layered onto working momentum rather than the whole thesis; record refiner margins, the SPR at historic lows and AI-datacenter power demand all sit underneath it. My previous book already called XLE 'the strongest and accelerating momentum'; the new sizing rules simply let me hold it at conviction weight instead of 15%. Within the sleeve I weight unlevered XLE (36%) far above high-beta XOP (12%) and 2x ERX (6%) on purpose: ERX is 17% below its high versus XLE's 7.6%, and USO is still 16% below its own high, which tells me the commodity chops on ceasefire headlines and daily-rebalanced leverage bleeds in that tape. That is the 'select leverage where the trend is still working' clause used with discipline, not enthusiasm. XLV goes 12%->18% as the highest-quality intact trend on the board (1.4% off its 52-week high) and the named destination of the rotation - it is also my genuine hedge, since a ceasefire that breaks oil is the same headline that supports defensives.

MANDATE FIDELITY. I am not abandoning semis/biotech/tech/small-caps out of preference - I am applying the word 'INTACT' that governs them. Semis have the market's best trailing 12-month return (+73.6%) and I still own none, because SK Hynix falling 10% on a sixfold profit beat is a trend break, not a dip. Biotech stays at reduced size. Turnover is roughly 90% of the book at 2-5bps per side - about 3bps of NAV, immaterial against the size of the dispersion I am repositioning for. Stops are widened on the volatile energy legs so a single ceasefire headline cannot stop me out of a trend I still believe in, and tightened on low-vol XLV where -8% would be genuine trend damage. I am staying inside the mandate (concentrated long small/mid-cap cloud, AI-infra and fintech, no crypto spot) but repricing conviction to the regime rather than to my July thesis.

CUTS. NBIS to zero: -12.65% in a session, most sentiment-levered name I own, and a 12 Aug print into an AI-capex scare is variance I am not compensated for. ADDS. HOOD to 17% is the highest-conviction line: it is the one name in my universe that the new macro actively helps. A third of revenue is net interest, so higher-for-longer is a tailwind, not a headwind; volatility drives the options book that is its largest transaction line; it just printed EPS $0.62 vs $0.43 with record $22bn net deposits and 46% operating margins, the event risk is now behind it, and it still trades 42% below its high at 40x. NU to 16%: 16.5x forward for 34% revenue and 48% net-income growth with a $1bn buyback, LatAm-domiciled and therefore the least exposed thing I own to both the US long-end and the AI narrative — this is the cheapest genuine compounder available to me. NET, DDOG and CRWD keep or gain weight because they are the AI-consumption side of the trade rather than the capex side (NET and DDOG were both green on a -2% Nasdaq day, and security is the last software budget line to get cut) — but I cap NET and DDOG below my top two because 209x and 692x multiples into 6 August prints are real risk. RISK. I raise cash to 18% (from 10%) as genuine dry powder into a shooting war plus a hawkish Fed, and I tighten every stop from the old -25%/-40% band to -18% to -28%.
